Trump's 50% tariffs take effect after US, Canada fail to reach trade deal

President Donald Trump's 50% tariffs on some Canadian goods took effect early Saturday morning, following the collapse of U.S.-Canada trade negotiations. Both sides blamed each other for the breakdown, with the U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer stating Canada walked away from a deal, while Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney accused the U.S. of making last-minute changes to the terms. The tariffs target a range of products, including food items and alcoholic beverages, and are expected to affect a fraction of U.S. imports from Canada. Canada announced it would retaliate with its own tariffs, matching the U.S. levies "dollar for dollar."

The trade dispute comes weeks after Trump imposed new tariffs on 60 trade partners, including the European Union. Trump had previously paused the 50% tariffs on Canada after claiming a preliminary deal had been reached, but the negotiations collapsed before the final agreement was finalized. Carney stated that the U.S. introduced new demands in the final hours of talks, which he described as a "power play" and an attempt to restrict Canada's ability to negotiate with other countries.

Where the accounts differ

ABC News and Fox Business both report that Canada suspended trade talks and would retaliate with tariffs, but differ on the amount of Canadian goods affected. ABC News states the tariffs would apply to roughly $28 billion in Canadian goods, while Fox Business mentions $20 billion. Additionally, Fox Business notes that Canada plans to match the tariffs "dollar for dollar to protect our workers and businesses," a claim not included in ABC News. NPR and Newsweek both mention the tariffs took effect at midnight, but Newsweek states the tariffs apply to $20 billion in goods, while ABC News and Fox Business cite $28 billion. BBC and Washington Examiner describe the breakdown of negotiations, with Washington Examiner specifying that Carney outlined three "last-minute changes" in U.S. terms, which are not detailed in other accounts. ABC News and Washington Examiner both mention the U.S. Trade Representative's office denying the last-minute changes, while Fox Business and Newsweek attribute the breakdown to the U.S. introducing new demands.

Sources ABC News · Fox Business · NPR · Newsweek · BBC · Washington Examiner

US judge strikes down Trump immigrant visa ban affecting 75 countries

A federal judge in Manhattan ruled against the State Department’s suspension of immigrant visas. The policy, introduced by the Trump administration, suspended visa processing for nationals of 75 countries, including Afghanistan, Iran, Russia, and Somalia. The judge, Jeannette Vargas, found the policy exceeded Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s statutory authority and violated the Immigration and Nationality Act. The ruling overturned visa denials based solely on the ban and required the State Department to review cases on an individual basis.

The State Department had argued that applicants from these countries were “at a high risk for becoming a public charge,” citing concerns about the use of public resources. The policy, which took effect in January, affected applicants from Latin American, Balkan, South Asian, African, Middle Eastern, and Caribbean countries. The administration has not yet commented on the ruling.

Where the accounts differ

Al Jazeera and UPI both state the policy affected 75 countries, while Mother Jones and Washington Examiner mention the policy affected “nearly 40% of the world’s countries.” Al Jazeera and UPI list specific countries, including Afghanistan, Iran, Russia, and Somalia, while Just The News and Washington Examiner also list these countries. Mother Jones and New York Post attribute the claim about “nearly 40% of the world’s countries” to the State Department, while Al Jazeera and UPI do not mention this figure. Washington Examiner and New York Post attribute the claim about “nearly 40% of the world’s countries” to the State Department, while Al Jazeera and UPI do not mention this figure.

Sources Al Jazeera · Mother Jones · Just The News · UPI · Washington Examiner · New York Post

US Postal Service shares mail-in ballot restrictions despite court ruling

The United States Postal Service (USPS) has published a final draft of its proposed rules to restrict the use of mail-in ballots under President Donald Trump. The rules have so far been blocked by the US court system. The USPS shared the 95-page update on Friday so that the rules can go into effect immediately if the existing court injunction is reversed. Under the proposed rules, the Postal Service will not distribute mail-in ballots in states that do not comply with federal demands for voter records. States would be required to identify to the USPS any voters who have requested mail-in ballots. They would also have to redesign the ballot envelopes to feature barcodes that the Postal Service could use to track and identify voting materials.

The USPS argued that such changes were necessary to ensure compliance with federal law. Critics have accused the Trump administration of seeking to exert federal oversight on election administration, a task that falls to the states under the US Constitution. They warn that the Postal Service could use the proposed rules to gather voter information and reject ballots in states that do not comply with Trump’s demands. Trump has sought to place additional restrictions on voting, based on false claims of widespread election fraud. He has continued to maintain that he was the rightful winner of the 2020 presidential election, a race he lost. Mail-in ballots have been a longstanding focus of Trump’s efforts to exert greater control over the electoral process.

Where the accounts differ

Al Jazeera and The Guardian both report that the USPS shared the 95-page update on Friday, but Al Jazeera states the rules are blocked by the court system, while The Guardian notes that two court orders currently block the changes from taking effect. UPI and Straight Arrow News both mention that the rule was published on Friday and that it is blocked by court injunctions, but UPI adds that the rule is an amended version of the initial proposal which received more than 200,000 comments during its review phase. Washington Examiner states that the rule will be released on Wednesday, while Just The News does not mention a release date. The Guardian and UPI both note that the USPS is ready to implement the new restrictions on mail-in voting if the court injunctions are lifted, while Al Jazeera and Straight Arrow News mention that the rule is not enforceable for this year’s midterms unless the court lifts the injunctions.

Sources Al Jazeera · The Guardian · UPI · Straight Arrow News · Washington Examiner · Just The News

Trump will kick off the IndyCar race in the Beast before cars zoom through Washington’s streets

President Donald Trump and first lady Melania Trump are scheduled to watch Sunday’s Freedom 250 Grand Prix as the cars whip through the city’s downtown, including a stretch along Pennsylvania Avenue not too far from the White House. Trump will lead a traditional prerace kickoff in his presidential limo. The open-wheel race, with cars whizzing past Washington’s monuments at speeds approaching 200 mph, is the latest of Trump’s celebrations this year to mark America’s 250th birthday. The event will also include a prerace show and flyovers of military aircraft.

The Freedom 250 Grand Prix is the first IndyCar race in Washington, D.C., with cars expected to reach speeds of up to 180 mph. The race will cover 250 miles over 147 laps, winding through the National Mall and past landmarks such as the Smithsonian museums and the Capitol building. The event is expected to attract about 140,000 people, with street closures and traffic disruptions planned for the weekend.

Where the accounts differ

The Associated Press reports that Trump will lead a prerace kickoff in his presidential limo, as stated by U.S. Ambassador Monica Crowley. Straight Arrow News mentions that Trump will take a ceremonial ride ahead of the main event, while the New York Post states he will drive the course in his armored limo “the Beast” on race day. The Christian Science Monitor notes that Trump signed an order calling for the race, while the CBS News account does not mention this. The Straight Arrow News includes quotes from Karen Jarussi and Colton Snedecor expressing differing opinions on the event, which are not present in the other accounts.

Sources Associated Press · Straight Arrow News · Christian Science Monitor · New York Post · CBS News

No source labeled lean-right or left covered this story.

TikTok agrees to $400m settlement to resolve US children’s privacy litigation

The U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) and TikTok, along with its parent company ByteDance, have reached a $400 million settlement to resolve allegations that the app violated children’s online privacy laws. The DOJ filed the lawsuit in 2024, accusing TikTok and ByteDance of failing to protect children’s privacy and collecting personal information from users under 13 without parental consent. Under the settlement, TikTok will pay $300 million immediately and an additional $100 million once a court vacates a prior consent decree from 2019 involving TikTok’s predecessor, Musical.ly. The DOJ stated that TikTok has made significant changes to its ownership, management, compliance functions, and privacy practices since the lawsuit began.

The settlement is described as one of the largest ever obtained in a case under the Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act (COPPA). The DOJ emphasized that the resolution ensures stronger protections for American families without prolonged litigation. TikTok’s U.S. joint venture, established in 2024, requires users to enter their date of birth to use the app and claims to have systems in place to identify and delete underage accounts.

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian and Axios both state that TikTok did not immediately comment, while Fox Business and Straight Arrow News mention that TikTok did not respond to their requests for comment. The Guardian and BBC note that the settlement only involves TikTok’s operations in China, whereas the Washington Examiner and Fox Business do not specify this limitation. The BBC and Washington Examiner mention the $5.7 million fine paid by Musical.ly in 2019, while the Guardian and Axios do not include this detail. The Guardian and BBC attribute the statement about TikTok’s age-moderation systems to a court filing, while the Washington Examiner and Fox Business attribute similar claims to the DOJ. The Straight Arrow News includes a quote from U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche, which is not present in other accounts.

Sources The Guardian · Axios · BBC · Washington Examiner · Fox Business · Straight Arrow News

No source labeled right covered this story.

Pentagon fires Stars and Stripes editor-in-chief, publisher, and reporter

The Pentagon has fired Erik Slavin, the editor-in-chief of Stars and Stripes, along with publisher Max Lederer and Middle East reporter Lara Korte. The firings were cited as insubordination, according to multiple accounts. Slavin, who has worked at the military newspaper for 21 years, stated he was fired for expressing concerns about potential censorship by the Pentagon. Korte, who covers the Middle East for Stars and Stripes, said she was informed she was fired for insubordination after telling a CBS reporter she works for the newspaper, not the Pentagon or any administration. Lederer, who had announced his retirement, also received a separation notice. Stars and Stripes, a military newspaper partially funded by the Department of Defense, has long maintained editorial independence, though it has faced pressure from the Pentagon to align its content with certain priorities.

Stars and Stripes, founded in 1861, has a history of editorial independence, including during World War I when it was revived under General John Pershing. The paper has been published continuously since World War II and is known for representing "the free thought and free expression of a free people." However, in January 2026, Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell posted on X that the department was modernizing Stars and Stripes, refocusing its content away from "woke distractions" that "syphon morale." The paper's independence was further challenged in March 2026 with a memo from the deputy secretary of defense that placed new restrictions on the paper's operations, including barring it from running comics and news from paid wire services.

Where the accounts differ

CBS News states that the Pentagon rescinded a federal regulation that required Stars and Stripes to operate "without news management or censorship," while UPI and Straight Arrow News report that the Pentagon described the firings as insubordination. The Daily Caller and UPI mention that the Pentagon fired three key figures, including Lederer, while CBS News and BBC note that Lederer had announced his retirement before being fired. The BBC also mentions that Slavin was considering his response to the firing notice, which is not explicitly stated in other accounts. The Daily Caller and Straight Arrow News report that the Pentagon installed a new deputy publisher, Capt. William Urban, before Lederer's firing, while CBS News and UPI do not mention this detail.

Sources CBS News · The Daily Caller · UPI · Straight Arrow News · BBC

No source labeled lean-right or left covered this story.

Prosecutors In Karmelo Anthony Case Hid The Most Damning Evidence

Karmelo Anthony, a 19-year-old high school student, was convicted of murdering 17-year-old Austin Metcalf during a track meet altercation in April 2025. The conviction led to a 35-year prison sentence. Anthony’s legal team is now seeking a new trial, arguing that critical evidence was withheld from the jury. Prosecutors disclosed during a hearing that they possessed text messages and photos that could have supported their case, including a message from Anthony to his ex-girlfriend describing his mental state on the day of the killing. The defense claims Anthony was coerced into waiving his right to testify and that the trial was unfair due to judicial bias.

Where the accounts differ

The Daily Wire and New York Post both report that Anthony sent a text message to his ex-girlfriend on the morning of the stabbing, including a photo of his knife with the caption “I’m low key on the verge.” The New York Post adds that Anthony also sent a text in 2023 stating, “imma shoot the school up tmr.” The UPI and CBS News do not mention these specific texts. The Daily Wire and FOX News both state that prosecutors disclosed a text where Anthony fantasized about stabbing someone and licking the blood off the blade, though the New York Post and CBS News do not include this detail. The Daily Wire and FOX News describe the evidence as a “confession” and “overwhelmingly beneficial to the prosecution’s case,” while the New York Post and CBS News do not make such characterizations. The UPI and CBS News do not mention the “gentleman’s agreement” between prosecutors and defense lawyers, while the Daily Wire, FOX News, and New York Post do.

Sources The Daily Wire · UPI · FOX News · New York Post · CBS News

No source labeled lean-right or left covered this story.

U.S. and Iran escalate economic tensions with sanctions and retaliatory threats

The U.S. has intensified its economic pressure on Iran, with President Trump vowing to launch the "most crushing economic operation ever taken against any country" and threatening "tremendous economic consequences" for any nation that supports Iran. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent described the measures as the "greatest coordinated economic isolation in the history of the world." Iran has responded by warning that any country joining the U.S. economic war will be considered an enemy and face retaliation. Iranian officials, including Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and Supreme National Security Council Secretary Mohsen Rezaei, have condemned the sanctions as "economic terrorism" and a violation of international law. The U.S. naval blockade and restrictions on the Strait of Hormuz, a key oil shipping route, have further strained relations. Diplomatic efforts to revive peace talks have stalled, with the 60-day memorandum of understanding to negotiate an end to the war expiring.

Iran's parliamentary speaker, Mohammad Baqer Ghalibaf, has dismissed the U.S. economic strategy as evidence of Washington's inability to prevail militarily, calling it a "cognitive war." Meanwhile, Iran has allowed some Iraqi oil tankers to transit the Strait of Hormuz, though it has not fully reopened the waterway.

Where the accounts differ

NPR reports that Trump called the sanctions an "economic D-Day" and that Bessent threatened secondary sanctions on nations, not just businesses. Al Jazeera states that Bessent said China was the "only country Bessent mentioned by name" and that China buys "about 90 percent" of Iranian oil. CBS News mentions that Iran's president acknowledged citizens face "many problems" and that Iran executed a man accused of carrying a chainsaw during protests. Straight Arrow News adds that Iranian officials rejected the sanctions as "economic warfare" and that Bessent described the measures as part of "the greatest coordinated economic isolation in the history of the world." The Guardian notes that Trump claimed the Strait of Hormuz is a "new US territory" and that Rezaei warned of targeting oil-shipping routes if neighbors join the U.S. economic war.

Sources NPR · Al Jazeera · CBS News · Straight Arrow News · The Guardian

No source labeled lean-right or right covered this story.

Below the fold — the model's one nomination, reason printed: Drastic water cuts issued for California, Nevada and Arizona from Colorado River threaten millions with severe drought impacts on health, agriculture, and daily life.

Drastic water cuts issued for California, Nevada and Arizona from Colorado River

Federal officials announced sharp water cuts for the next two years for three Western states that rely on the Colorado River. Under the Bureau of Reclamation's plan, California, Nevada and Arizona will collectively reduce water use by 1.25 million acre-feet annually during that period, with the possibility of larger cuts depending on conditions. Arizona will see the biggest cuts, while states upstream — Colorado, Utah, Wyoming and New Mexico — do not face any for now. Meanwhile, neighboring Mexico will reduce its intake by 250,000 acre-feet under a U.S.-Mexico treaty. The Colorado River serves as a water supply source to an estimated 35 million to 40 million people, according to the Bureau of Reclamation. The current rules governing the use of the river's water are set to expire in October, and the seven states have been unable to reach a consensus on sharing it over the long term. Last winter saw the worst snowpack on record for the Colorado River Basin, adding more stress on farmers, industry, wildlife and hydropower producers, as well as tens of millions of people who rely on the waterway, including in dozens of Native American tribes and in two Mexican states.

Where the accounts differ

CBS News states that Arizona will see the biggest cuts, while ABC News specifies that Arizona will face a reduction of 760,000 acre-feet, California 440,000 acre-feet, and Nevada 50,000 acre-feet. UPI also reports these specific reductions, aligning with ABC News. CBS News does not mention the breakdown of cuts among the states, only that Arizona will see the biggest cuts. ABC News and UPI both mention the 1.25 million acre-feet total reduction, but ABC News adds that the DOI encourages the three states to "voluntarily conserve and store at least 700,000 acre-feet of water over the two-year period to protect the system, in addition to the 1.25 million acre-feet per year of reductions." CBS News does not mention this voluntary conservation target. UPI does not mention the voluntary conservation target or the breakdown of cuts among the states.

Sources CBS News · ABC News · UPI

No source labeled lean-right or left or right covered this story.

New details about Trump's plans for Kennedy Center and White House ballroom

President Trump's plans for the John F. Kennedy Memorial Center for the Performing Arts and the White House ballroom are moving forward despite ongoing legal challenges. Court filings reveal that the Kennedy Center's board, dominated by Trump allies, has approved a plan to rename the building in his honor and include his name on its facade. The board also intends to rename the physical site "President Donald J. Trump Plaza." Meanwhile, the White House ballroom project, which involves millions of pounds of steel and rebar, is proceeding with a crew of over 200 workers. The Supreme Court has temporarily allowed construction to continue, though the legality of the project remains in question.

The Kennedy Center's board has faced legal challenges after a judge ruled their previous decision to name the building after Trump was unlawful. The board has now voted to add Trump's name to the building's facade, with plans to update the inscription once a $100 million fund is reached. The Justice Department stated that the tarp covering the facade is due to water testing and structural repairs, though the exact duration of the tarp's presence remains unclear.

Where the accounts differ

CBS News reports that the Kennedy Center's board is stacked with Trump allies and that the tarp is due to water testing and structural repairs. The Nation claims the tarp was used to remove Trump's name from the building and that the marble may have been damaged. The New York Post states that the Supreme Court allowed the ballroom construction to continue, while The Daily Wire and Axios focus on unrelated stories about a Cambridge professor and a scholar's suspension. NPR and Axios both report that the Supreme Court allowed the ballroom construction to proceed, but Axios adds that the project's cost is projected to be at least $600 million.

Sources CBS News · The Nation · New York Post · The Daily Wire · NPR · Axios

Charter plane crash kills 8 near remote radar site in western Alaska, military says

A charter aircraft carrying eight people crashed at a remote radar site in western Alaska on Thursday, killing all on board, the US military said. The crash occurred near Cape Newenham Long Range Radar Site Airport, approximately 450 miles west of Anchorage, Alaska. The plane, a Cessna 441, had taken off from Anchorage and was believed to have crashed early Thursday afternoon on approach to Cape Newenham. The Federal Aviation Administration confirmed the crash happened about 12:15 p.m. Thursday west of Cape Newenham. The National Transportation Safety Board’s Alaska region chief, Clint Johnson, stated there were two pilots and six passengers on board.

The crash site is managed by the Pacific Air Forces Regional Support Center and is part of a network of remote radar sites that tracks aircraft operating in Alaska’s airspace and along its borders. The US military described those on board as “dedicated professionals carrying out a vital mission in a demanding environment.” The US Army Corps of Engineers confirmed two of its employees were among those killed, and the NTSB and FAA are investigating the crash.

Where the accounts differ

The New York Post and NPR report the crash occurred near Cape Newenham Long Range Radar Site Airport, while the Daily Wire and CBS News specify it was near the same location. The Daily Caller reports a midair collision between a civilian plane and a police helicopter in Pennsylvania, which is a different incident. The Daily Wire and CBS News mention the plane was carrying Army engineers, while the New York Post and NPR do not specify the identities of the victims. The Daily Wire and CBS News attribute the cause of the crash to a military mission, while the New York Post and NPR do not provide details on the specific work the individuals were doing. The Daily Wire and CBS News state that two Army Corps of Engineers employees were among the victims, while the New York Post and NPR do not specify the identities of the victims.

Sources New York Post · The Daily Caller · The Daily Wire · NPR · CBS News · UPI

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

Trump's 50% tariffs take effect after US, Canada fail to reach trade deal

The U.S. and Canada failed to reach a trade deal, leading to the imposition of 50% tariffs on Canadian goods. The tariffs, targeting a range of products including food items and alcoholic beverages, took effect at 12:01 a.m. ET on Saturday. Both sides blamed each other for the breakdown in negotiations. U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer stated that Canada declined to finalize the trade deal under the terms agreed earlier in the week, while Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney suspended trade talks, citing "last-minute changes" to U.S. proposed terms as unfair and uneconomic. Canada vowed to retaliate with dollar-for-dollar tariffs.

Where the accounts differ

ABC News and Fox Business both mention that the tariffs would apply to roughly $28 billion of Canadian goods, while CBS News and The Guardian state the figure is about $20 billion. Fox Business and The Guardian attribute the breakdown to "last-minute changes" in U.S. proposed terms, while ABC News and CBS News report that Canada made last-minute changes. The Guardian and CBS News note that the tariffs would affect about 5% of Canadian exports to the U.S., a detail not included in ABC News or Fox Business. The Guardian and CBS News also mention that the tariffs were initially scheduled to take effect at 12:01 a.m. Wednesday but were delayed for three days, a detail not present in ABC News or Fox Business.

Sources ABC News · Fox Business · NPR · Just The News · The Guardian · CBS News

Lindsay Clancy faces murder trial after killing three children

Lindsay Clancy, 36, is on trial for the deaths of her three children, Cora, Dawson, and Callan, who were found strangled at their Massachusetts home in January 2023. The prosecution claims she intentionally killed them, while her defense argues she suffered from postpartum psychosis. Clancy, who is paralyzed from a fall after the incident, has been attending the trial in a wheelchair. Her ex-husband, Patrick Clancy, testified in court, describing his emotional struggle and his subsequent remarriage. The trial has sparked broader discussions about maternal mental health and the treatment of postpartum psychosis.

Where the accounts differ

The Daily Wire reports that the "same, Lindsay" trend on TikTok is a misconception, noting that the ice-throwing mom video was uploaded in 2024, years before the trial began. The Free Press highlights a growing online movement of women who believe Clancy is innocent and that her husband committed the crime, a claim not mentioned in the Associated Press or BBC accounts. The Guardian and BBC both mention the defense's argument that Clancy suffered from postpartum psychosis, while FOX News adds details about Patrick Clancy's remarriage and relocation to New York City, which are not included in the other accounts.

Sources Associated Press · The Daily Wire · FOX News · The Free Press · The Guardian · BBC

Trump to speak in South Carolina at Darline Graham rally

President Donald Trump will visit South Carolina Friday to support Sen. Darline Graham in her Senate bid. Graham, who was appointed to finish her brother's term after his death, faces a Republican primary runoff on Tuesday against Rep. Ralph Norman. Trump's endorsement of Graham has been a key part of her campaign, though she did not win a majority in the Aug. 11 primary, requiring a runoff. Graham's campaign has focused on issues like the SAVE America Act and transgender athletes, while also addressing national security, though she admitted she is not well-versed in the subject. Trump has emphasized the importance of her election for his policies, warning that losing the Senate race would mean losing tax cuts and border control.

Graham's debate performance, where she admitted lacking expertise on national security, has drawn criticism. Former South Carolina Gov. Nikki Haley, who supports Norman, criticized her lack of knowledge, noting that her late brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham, was well-informed on such matters. Graham has defended her honesty, stating she is not a politician and is willing to learn. Trump has also urged voters to "pretend" he is on the ballot to boost turnout, claiming his presence will help secure her victory.

Where the accounts differ

UPI reports that Graham received 33% of the vote in the Aug. 11 primary, while CBS News states she received 32.7%. UPI also mentions that Graham's campaign is relying on more than just Trump's endorsement, a detail not included in the other accounts. The Washington Examiner highlights Trump's focus on voting requirements and transgender issues, which are not mentioned in UPI or CBS News. FOX News emphasizes Graham's lack of national security knowledge and contrasts it with her brother's expertise, a point not made in UPI or CBS News. Just The News and the New York Post both report Trump's "pretend I'm on the ballot" comment, while UPI and CBS News do not mention this specific line.

Sources UPI · Washington Examiner · FOX News · Just The News · New York Post · CBS News

No source labeled left covered this story.

IndyCars set to race on streets of nation's capital. Here's what to know

IndyCars will race on the streets of Washington, D.C., for the first time during the Freedom 250 Grand Prix, a 250-mile event celebrating the country's 250th birthday. The race will take place on Sunday, with practice and qualifying runs on Saturday. The 1.66-mile track will include Pennsylvania Avenue and Independence Avenue, with speeds expected to exceed 180 mph. The event is expected to draw about 140,000 spectators each day, with free tickets distributed through a lottery. President Donald Trump is expected to attend, and the race is supported by the White House and IndyCar, which is owned by Penske Entertainment Corp. Organizers have resurfaced roadways and welded over 200 manhole covers shut to prevent them from flying off during the race. The event is part of a series of celebrations for the 250th anniversary of America's independence.

Organizers have also constructed risers for spectators and bridges to allow people to navigate the closed streets. The event is being run by the Freedom 250 Grand Prix organization, which is supported by key partners including IndyCar's promotional alliance with Monumental Sports & Entertainment. The race is not without controversy, as some preservationists have raised concerns about potential damage to historic buildings and art due to vibrations from the race. The U.S. Capitol and other historic sites are located near the race course.

Where the accounts differ

ABC News reports that the race will be broadcast live on Fox, while Just The News states that the race will be covered by The Center Square. Christian Science Monitor mentions that the event is part of Trump's Freedom 250 celebrations, which include mixed martial arts events, a detail not included in ABC News. Straight Arrow News includes quotes from Karen Jarussi and Colton Snedecor, which are not present in other accounts. New York Post and Straight Arrow News both mention Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy's comments about the event bringing America together, but only New York Post provides specific details about Duffy's interview. Just The News states that the event is part of over $90 million in taxpayer funds spent on America's 250th anniversary celebrations, a figure not mentioned in other accounts. Christian Science Monitor and Straight Arrow News both mention concerns about the race's impact on historic sites, but only Christian Science Monitor includes quotes from political strategist Michael Caputo and political commentator Chris Cillizza.

Sources ABC News · Christian Science Monitor · NPR · New York Post · Straight Arrow News · Just The News

No source labeled left covered this story.

Florida’s GOP Uses Socialist Label Against Democratic Candidates in Primary

In Florida, the Republican Party has launched a campaign against Democratic candidates by labeling them as socialists, a strategy seen at a GOP victory rally where Sen. Ashley Moody and Rep. Byron Donalds spoke. Moody, the GOP Senate nominee, accused Democratic state Rep. Angie Nixon of wanting to turn the U.S. into Cuba, despite Nixon's campaign focusing on affordability, Medicare for all, and free childcare. The rally marked the GOP's start for the general election, with Republicans using the socialist label to stoke fears against their opponents. Rep. Byron Donalds, who won the Republican nomination for governor, called Nixon a "Trojan horse" for the Democratic Socialists of America, even though she is not affiliated with the group.

Angie Nixon, a Democratic Socialists of America member, won a surprising primary victory over former Trump impeachment witness Alex Vindman. Nixon's win is being seen as a DSA victory, though the organization did not endorse her. She has since distanced herself from DSA orthodoxy, stating she is not a socialist and does not support defunding police or open borders. Nixon's campaign has focused on issues like affordability and healthcare, positioning her as a progressive but not a traditional socialist.

Where the accounts differ

Mother Jones reports that Nixon is a member of the Democratic Socialists of America and that the GOP used the socialist label against her, while FOX News highlights Nixon's primary win as a DSA victory and notes her defeat of Vindman despite being outspent. The New York Post mentions Nixon's accusation that Republicans are "literally trying to kill" black Americans, which the Department of Homeland Security rejected. Axios states Nixon is not a socialist and has distanced herself from DSA orthodoxy, while The Daily Wire reports Nixon called Charlie Kirk supporters tools of "white supremacy." BBC notes Nixon's win as part of a trend of left-wing insurgents defeating centrist candidates.

Sources Mother Jones · FOX News · New York Post · Axios · The Daily Wire · BBC

Trump tells Michael Cohen he was ‘weaponized’ in hush money trial

President Donald Trump praised his former lawyer Michael Cohen for recanting his 2024 testimony in Trump’s hush money trial, calling the justice system “weaponized” against Cohen. Their first public conversation in eight years took place during a radio interview on 77WABC, where Trump referred to Cohen as “boss” and acknowledged his former lawyer’s “recanted everything you said.” Cohen, who once testified against Trump in the hush money case, described his relationship with Trump as a “path of darkness” in 2018 but later claimed he felt “pressured and coerced” by prosecutors.

In the interview, Trump claimed that Cohen had been unfairly threatened with jail by prosecutors who used his testimony to convict Trump of campaign finance violations and fraud. Cohen, who served prison time for his role in the hush money payments, is seeking a presidential pardon and has applied for one, though he has not yet received confirmation.

Where the accounts differ

The Washington Examiner reports that Trump specifically accused New York Attorney General Letitia James and Manhattan prosecutor Alvin Bragg of weaponizing the justice system against Cohen, while The Guardian and Straight Arrow News do not mention these prosecutors by name. The New York Post states that Cohen plans to call the Justice Department tomorrow to check on his pardon application, a detail not included in the other accounts. The Guardian also notes that Cohen has not necessarily recanted everything he said about Trump, a point not raised by the other outlets.

Sources The Guardian · Washington Examiner · New York Post · Straight Arrow News

No source labeled lean-left covered this story.

Below the fold — the model's one nomination, reason printed: World Bank projects war-hit Lebanon’s economy to contract by 6.4 percent, threatening livelihoods and exacerbating poverty for millions.

World Bank projects war-hit Lebanon’s economy to contract by 6.4 percent

The World Bank reported that Lebanon’s economy is projected to shrink by 6.4 percent in 2026 due to the ongoing conflict with Israel, which has disrupted the country’s fragile recovery. The report noted that Lebanon entered 2026 on stronger footing after a 4.2 percent GDP growth in 2025, the highest since the 2019 financial crisis. The conflict, which escalated in March 2026, has damaged housing and infrastructure, displaced communities, and disrupted supply chains, tourism, and domestic demand. Inflation is expected to rise to 17.5 percent, driven by supply disruptions, higher shipping costs, and volatile fuel prices.

The report highlights that Lebanon’s economic recovery has been sharply interrupted by the renewed conflict, exacerbating an already severe social and economic crisis. The World Bank emphasized the importance of advancing reforms, particularly in banking sector restructuring and fiscal management, to restore confidence and support reconstruction. The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has endorsed legislative progress on financial sector reforms and plans to resume technical meetings in Beirut to evaluate further structural measures.

Where the accounts differ

Al Jazeera reports that the conflict escalation occurred in March 2026 and that 1.2 million people were displaced, while UPI states that the conflict began on March 2 and that 4,348 people have been killed and 12,703 injured since March 2. UPI also provides casualty figures and mentions the Lebanese Health Ministry’s latest count, which Al Jazeera does not include. UPI notes that Lebanon’s government recorded a 3.9% GDP surplus in 2025, a detail absent in Al Jazeera’s account. Al Jazeera mentions the IMF’s endorsement of legislative progress and its planned technical meetings, while UPI includes additional context about the financial crisis and the impact of the conflict on public finances.

Sources Al Jazeera · UPI

No source labeled lean-right or left or right covered this story.

The brief ends here.

Trump orders reduction of U.S.-South Korea drills, citing North Korea concerns

U.S. President Donald Trump announced on Monday that the Pentagon should “substantially reduce” the annual joint military exercises between the United States and South Korea, which were set to begin on Monday. The order came via Trump’s Truth Social platform, with the president describing the drills as sending an “inappropriate and hostile” signal to North Korea. The drills, known as Ulchi Freedom Shield, were initially scheduled to last 11 days, but by Wednesday, the U.S. and South Korea had agreed to cut the exercise to five days and scale back some field training drills. South Korean officials expressed surprise at the lack of prior notice, with Foreign Minister Cho Hyun stating that neither the government nor U.S. officials were informed of Trump’s directive in advance.

The decision has sparked debate in South Korea over the reliability of the U.S. security guarantee, which has been a cornerstone of the alliance since the Korean War. South Korean President Lee Jae Myung called for strengthening the country’s self-reliant defense capabilities while expressing support for the U.S.-South Korea alliance. However, some South Korean lawmakers and citizens have criticized Trump’s approach, with one user on social media stating, “We can’t trust everything Trump says.”

Where the accounts differ

Al Jazeera reports that Trump’s order was made public via his Truth Social platform, while ABC News states that the announcement was made via a press availability on Monday. UPI and Washington Examiner both note that Trump cited a “good relationship” with Kim Jong Un as a reason for the reduction, but Al Jazeera and Mother Jones attribute this claim to Trump directly, while UPI and Washington Examiner attribute it to U.S. officials. Mother Jones and Associated Press mention that North Korea launched a missile barrage the day after the drills were scaled back, while Al Jazeera and UPI do not mention the missile launches. Al Jazeera and Mother Jones include quotes from South Korean officials and citizens, while ABC News and UPI focus more on the statements from North Korea and the U.S. government.

Sources Al Jazeera · ABC News · UPI · Washington Examiner · Mother Jones · Associated Press

Socialist Scores Major Upset, Stuns Trump Impeachment Witness In Senate Primary

Florida state Rep. Angie Nixon defeated former Trump impeachment witness Alex Vindman in the Democratic Senate primary. Nixon, a member of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), will face Sen. Ashley Moody (R-FL) in November. Vindman, who testified against Trump during his first impeachment, raised significantly more money than Nixon, with $16.3 million compared to Nixon’s $975,000. Nixon’s victory is seen as a boost for the Democratic Party’s Left-wing and a potential challenge for Republicans in a state Trump won by 13 points in 2024. Nixon received endorsements from far-Left lawmakers including Reps. Maxwell Frost (D-FL), Ilhan Omar (D-MN), and Rashida Tlaib (D-MI). Trump criticized Vindman on social media, calling him a “SleazeBag” and praising Nixon as a “Radical Left Lunatic.”

Nixon, a former union organizer, ran on an affordability platform including Medicare for All, free childcare, and a national rent freeze. She faced a trial in September for trespassing and resisting an officer during a sit-in protest at the governor’s office. Analysts have moved the Florida Senate race from “likely Republican” to “safe Republican” following her win. Nixon’s victory is part of a trend of progressive candidates winning primaries this cycle, including Michigan’s Abdul El-Sayed.

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian reports that Nixon was not endorsed by the DSA, while The Daily Wire and Mother Jones state she received endorsements from DSA members. The Guardian also mentions Nixon faces a trial for trespassing and resisting an officer, which is also noted by Mother Jones. The Free Press highlights that Nixon’s victory is seen as tone-deaf in South Florida, a region with many Cuban and Venezuelan voters who fled socialist regimes, while Axios notes that Nixon has distanced herself from DSA orthodoxy and does not identify as a socialist. The Daily Wire and The Guardian differ on the extent of Nixon’s alignment with DSA, with The Guardian stating she was not endorsed by the group, while The Daily Wire and Mother Jones note she received support from DSA-aligned figures.

Sources The Daily Wire · The Guardian · Mother Jones · NPR · Axios · The Free Press

FBI seizes Swalwell’s devices at airport as sexual misconduct investigation escalates: sources

Federal agents seized electronic devices from former Rep. Eric Swalwell at San Francisco International Airport on Saturday night, according to multiple sources. The FBI also executed a search warrant at Swalwell’s Washington, D.C., home the following day. The actions are part of an ongoing criminal probe into allegations of sexual misconduct against the former congressman. Swalwell resigned from Congress in April after facing multiple accusations of sexual misconduct and rape, including claims from a former staffer that he raped her twice when she was too intoxicated to consent. The FBI has not arrested or detained Swalwell in connection with the investigation.

Swalwell, who represented Bay Area districts from 2013 until his resignation, had previously faced scrutiny over his relationship with Christine "Fang Fang" Fang, a suspected Chinese intelligence operative. Declassified documents released by the White House in July revealed that Swalwell had "physical relations" with Fang on several occasions, including in March 2015. The FBI first interviewed Swalwell in May 2015 and again in March 2016 regarding the relationship. The White House’s Government Transparency Task Force released the documents, which were previously reported by The Daily Mail and CBS News.

Where the accounts differ

FOX News and ABC News both report that Swalwell was not arrested or detained during the FBI seizure. CBS News and UPI do not mention whether he was detained, though CBS News specifies that an iPhone and a MacBook Pro were seized. The Daily Wire and NPR do not mention the specific devices seized, though NPR notes that the seizure was confirmed by an anonymous AP source. ABC News and CBS News both state that Swalwell resigned from Congress in April, while FOX News and UPI mention that he resigned after facing expulsion efforts. The Daily Wire and NPR provide more detail on the nature of the allegations, including specific claims of rape and unsolicited explicit messages.

Sources FOX News · The Daily Wire · NPR · ABC News · CBS News · UPI

Prince Harry and Meghan moving back to Britain this month

Prince Harry and Meghan, the Duke and Duchess of Sussex, are planning to return to live in Britain, six years after leaving for the US. The couple and their two children, Prince Archie, seven, and Princess Lilibet, five, are expected to relocate later in August to a non-royal residence outside London. The children are enrolled to start school in September. King Charles was reportedly informed on Sunday that his son and daughter-in-law would return to Britain. The Sussexes, who have lived in California since 2020, had a reunion with the king last month at Highgrove in Gloucestershire. The couple will not be offered a “half-in half-out” option, which was rejected by Queen Elizabeth II in 2020. The Sussexes are expected to retain their homes in California and Portugal. Their security arrangements have not been disclosed, and they are not eligible for taxpayer-funded protection in the UK, except when within royal residences.

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian and Washington Examiner both mention that the Sussexes are expected to relocate later in August, while CBS News and The Daily Wire refer to the move as happening "this month" or "later this month." The Guardian and NPR state that the children are enrolled to start school in September, while CBS News and The Daily Wire do not specify the exact month for school enrollment. The Guardian and Washington Examiner note that the couple will not be offered a “half-in half-out” option, while The Daily Wire and CBS News do not mention this detail. The Guardian and NPR report that Harry and Meghan visited the UK last month, while CBS News and Washington Examiner mention that they traveled to the UK last month to promote the 2027 Invictus Games. The Guardian and Washington Examiner state that the king is said to welcome the opportunity to see more of his family, while CBS News and The Daily Wire do not mention this.

Sources The Guardian · NPR · CBS News · BBC · Washington Examiner · The Daily Wire

Mike Rogers backs data center moratorium as some GOP candidates shift against AI

Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers in Michigan has endorsed a one-year moratorium on new data center expansion, aligning with a policy backed by politicians across the aisle. Rogers expressed concerns about the rapid spread of AI infrastructure and called for a pause to address public questions. The issue has become a focal point in the 2026 midterm elections, with voters raising concerns about the impact of data centers on power grids and water supplies. Meanwhile, Democratic candidate Abdul el Sayed has called for a halt to data center development until federal regulations are in place.

Data centers have become a divisive issue in the midterm elections, particularly in Midwestern states. A Politico/Public First poll from July showed declining public support for data centers, especially among Democrats. The National Republican Senatorial Committee has warned AI companies about the growing opposition, noting that Democrats have been campaigning on this issue. Some GOP candidates, like Rep. Tom Tiffany, have also adopted anti-data center rhetoric in their campaigns.

Where the accounts differ

The Washington Examiner and ABC News both mention the data center issue in Ohio, but differ on the specifics of the political race. The Washington Examiner states that the race is for Sen. Gary Peters’s seat, while ABC News refers to the race for Sen. Jon Husted’s seat. The Washington Examiner also notes that Gov. Kathy Hochul implemented a moratorium in New York, a detail not included in ABC News. The Daily Caller and Mother Jones both reference a leaked NRSC memo, but the Daily Caller attributes the memo to Axios, while Mother Jones does not specify the source of the memo. The Axios article provides detailed statistics on data center water and energy use, which are not included in the other accounts.

Sources Washington Examiner · Axios · ABC News · Mother Jones · The Daily Caller · Newsweek

FBI arrests woman over alleged plot to bomb New York state capitol building

The FBI arrested Jessica Bowie, 35, of Albany, New York, for allegedly plotting to bomb the New York State Capitol building. According to a criminal complaint, Bowie, who converted to Islam five years ago and used the Islamic name "Aisha Saif," communicated with FBI informants posing as ISIS members. She allegedly discussed using a DoorDash delivery bag to hide an explosive device and planned to attack the Capitol on a day when the most senators would be present. Bowie also allegedly expressed interest in future attacks, including on the White House and New Year’s Eve celebrations in Times Square. The FBI claims she purchased bomb-making materials from a Home Depot in Rensselaer, New York, and had an escape plan to Syria. Bowie allegedly told informants she wanted to destroy as much of the Capitol as possible and kill senators, and that she would return to the U.S. to carry out more attacks.

Where the accounts differ

The New York Post and FOX News both mention Bowie’s alleged plan to attack the White House and Times Square, while the BBC and UPI do not specify these targets. The New York Post and CBS News state that Bowie allegedly discussed returning to the U.S. to carry out more attacks, while the BBC and UPI do not mention this. The Al Jazeera article notes that Bowie was charged with providing material support for terrorism, while the New York Post and CBS News mention the specific charge of attempting to provide material support for foreign terrorist organizations. The UPI and BBC report that Bowie was given an inert explosive device and a non-working handgun by informants, which is not mentioned in the other accounts.

Sources New York Post · Al Jazeera · CBS News · BBC · UPI · FOX News

No source labeled left covered this story.

Aisha Wahab wins California House special election in defiance of AIPAC money flood

Democratic state Sen. Aisha Wahab won the special election for former Rep. Eric Swalwell’s seat in California’s 14th Congressional District. Wahab earned 53.1% of the vote, according to the Associated Press, after winning the primary by 26 points. Her opponent, Melissa Hernandez, a moderate Democrat and former Bay Area Rapid Transit director, received 46.9% of the vote. Wahab will serve in the House of Representatives until January and will face Hernandez again in the November election for a full two-year term. The seat was vacated when Swalwell resigned in April due to sexual misconduct allegations, which he has denied. The FBI seized Swalwell’s electronic devices as part of a federal criminal investigation.

The race was marked by significant outside spending, with AIPAC-linked super PACs pouring millions into the race. The Washington Examiner reported that AIPAC spent $4.4 million against Wahab, while CBS News noted that over $4 million was spent on the race since last month, with about $3.7 million going to Hernandez’s campaign. The Guardian and The New York Post both mentioned that AIPAC-backed groups spent over $5 million on pro-Hernandez ads and Wahab attack ads. The race also saw accusations of election violations, with Wahab alleging fake social media posts and Hernandez accusing Wahab of illegally transferring campaign funds.

Where the accounts differ

The Washington Examiner and The Guardian both report that AIPAC spent $4.4 million against Wahab, while CBS News states that over $4 million was spent on the race since last month, with $3.7 million going to Hernandez’s campaign. The New York Post mentions that AIPAC-backed groups spent over $5 million on pro-Hernandez ads and Wahab attack ads, which is not explicitly stated in the other accounts. The Guardian and The New York Post also note that Wahab was the first Muslim elected to the California Senate, a detail not included in the Washington Examiner or CBS News accounts. The FOX News account mentions that Wahab received 42.8% of the vote in the special primary against Hernandez’s 16.8%, a figure not provided by other outlets.

Sources Washington Examiner · New York Post · The Guardian · CBS News · Just The News · FOX News

Lindsay Clancy trial continues as defense presents new witness

Lindsay Clancy's murder trial in Massachusetts continued with the defense calling a forensic psychologist to testify about her mental state. The prosecution had previously concluded its case, and the defense is now seeking to present additional evidence. A TikTok user who worked at McLean Hospital was initially considered as a witness but was ruled ineligible by the judge. The trial has drawn significant public attention, with social media users and experts debating the case. The defense argues that Clancy suffered from postpartum psychosis, while prosecutors claim she acted deliberately. The trial has also sparked discussions about mental health and the legal system's handling of such cases.

Where the accounts differ

The Associated Press omits any mention of the trial or Lindsay Clancy, focusing instead on other news stories. The Daily Wire presents a highly critical and opinionated view of the trial, suggesting that women are rallying behind Clancy due to social media influence and that the trial is a reflection of broader societal issues. Slate provides a more balanced perspective, discussing the complexities of motherhood and the case as part of a broader narrative about maternal struggles. CBS News details the trial proceedings, including the dismissal of a potential witness and the judge's ruling. BBC explains the legal and medical context of postpartum psychosis, while FOX News highlights the defense attorney's criticism of the prosecution's approach and includes specific examples of courtroom interactions.

Sources Associated Press · The Daily Wire · Slate · CBS News · BBC · FOX News

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

The brief ends here.

Trump Vows Unprecedented Economic Measures Against Iran Amid Stalled Talks

President Donald Trump announced on Wednesday that the United States is launching a new economic campaign against Iran, calling it "the MOST CRUSHING ECONOMIC OPERATION EVER TAKEN AGAINST ANY COUNTRY." The move comes after a 60-day ceasefire expired without a diplomatic resolution to the war that began in late February. Trump warned that any country aiding Iran financially would face "TREMENDOUS Economic Consequences," though he did not specify the measures. The administration has been applying economic pressure on Iran since April, aiming to cut off its revenue streams and isolate the country. The U.S. has also imposed a naval blockade on the Strait of Hormuz, a critical oil route, which has significantly impacted Iran's economy.

The economic measures are part of a broader strategy to weaken Iran's ability to sustain its military and economic operations. Reports indicate that Iran's oil production has dropped by nearly 23 percent since the start of the conflict, reducing its ability to generate foreign currency. The U.S. and its allies are seeking to maintain control over the Strait of Hormuz, which is vital for global oil trade. Trump claimed the U.S. has "complete control" of the strait, despite Iran's continued efforts to restrict maritime traffic through the region.

Where the accounts differ

Newsweek reports that Trump's economic measures are part of "Operation Economic Fury," which includes targeting oil smuggling, swap lines, and front companies. The Daily Wire adds that Trump's actions are aimed at dismantling Iran's "shadow economy," including illicit financial networks in China, Dubai, and Malaysia. BBC notes that the UAE has severed financial ties with Iran following a missile threat, while UPI mentions that China has been a major buyer of Iranian oil and has opposed U.S. sanctions. Washington Examiner highlights the financial impact of the naval blockade, estimating it could cost Iran $18 billion annually if continued.

Sources Newsweek · BBC · UPI · Washington Examiner · The Daily Wire · Axios

South Korea Wants Its Military Back

On August 27, 2025, ROK Army 7th Corps Engineer Brigade and U.S. Army 11th Engineer Battalion of the 2nd Infantry Division soldiers participated in a joint bridging drill in Yeoju, South Korea. South Korean President Lee Jae Myung reiterated calls for the country to regain full control of its military operations from the U.S. following Donald Trump’s order to cut back on annual joint training drills in preparation for North Korean threats. Trump cited his "very good relationship with Kim Jong Un" and South Korea’s refusal to support the U.S. war effort in Iran as reasons for reducing the drills. Lee responded by urging Seoul to plan a transfer of control over the Combined Forces Command, which oversees both South Korean and U.S. forces during wartime. South Korea has sought to regain wartime operational control since the 1950s Korean War, with regaining control seen as a key goal of Lee’s administration. Lee also signaled rearmament, including accelerating the development of nuclear-powered submarines.

Where the accounts differ

Mother Jones and ABC News both mention Trump’s claim that South Korea refused to support the U.S. war effort in Iran, while NPR and UPI attribute this claim to Trump. Al Jazeera and BBC attribute the claim to Trump as well, but BBC adds that Trump linked the decision to South Korea’s refusal to "give us a little hand" with Iran. Mother Jones and ABC News state that Trump cited his "very good relationship with Kim Jong Un" as a reason for reducing the drills, while NPR and UPI attribute this claim to Trump. Al Jazeera and BBC also attribute this claim to Trump, but BBC adds that Trump said Pyongyang had been "unthreatening and respectful" during his presidency. UPI and ABC News mention that Trump wrote on Truth Social that the drills "send a signal that is totally inappropriate and hostile" to North Korea, while Mother Jones and NPR attribute this statement to Trump. Al Jazeera and BBC also attribute this statement to Trump, but BBC adds that Trump said the drills were "costly" and "send a signal that is totally inappropriate and hostile" to North Korea.

Sources Mother Jones · NPR · Al Jazeera · ABC News · BBC · UPI

Prince Harry and Meghan leaving US for Britain after six-year royal feud

Prince Harry and Meghan Markle are relocating from the United States to the United Kingdom later this month, according to multiple outlets. The couple, along with their two children, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet, are expected to move to a private, non-royal residence outside London. The children are enrolled to start school in September. The move comes after a period of strained relations with the royal family, which began when the couple stepped down from their royal duties in 2020 and moved to California. The couple has not resumed their roles as working royals, and their status as private individuals remains unchanged.

The decision to return to the UK follows a meeting between Harry and King Charles III at Highgrove House in July, which marked the first time the king had seen his grandchildren in person in over four years. King Charles was reportedly informed of the couple’s plans on Sunday, and he has expressed willingness to see them in a private capacity. The move also comes after Harry expressed a desire for reconciliation with his family, particularly following his father’s diagnosis with an unspecified form of cancer.

Where the accounts differ

The Washington Examiner and The Guardian both state that King Charles was informed of the couple’s decision on Sunday, while The Daily Wire and BBC report that the king was made aware of the plans on Sunday as well. The Guardian and The Daily Wire mention that the couple’s return was not discussed during their July visit to Highgrove, whereas The Washington Examiner and BBC suggest that the visit was a key development in their relationship. The Daily Wire and The Guardian note that Harry has remained estranged from his brother, Prince William, while The Washington Examiner and BBC do not explicitly state this. The Daily Wire includes a quote from GB News commentator Patrick Christys, which is absent from other accounts.

Sources Washington Examiner · The Daily Wire · The Guardian · NPR · Just The News · BBC

Trump to tap Heidi Overton as FDA commissioner

President Trump has nominated White House aide Heidi Overton to lead the Food and Drug Administration, according to multiple outlets. Overton, currently deputy director of the White House Domestic Policy Council, was one of several candidates considered for the role. The nomination comes after former FDA commissioner Marty Makary resigned in May following clashes with the Trump administration over the safety of flavored vapes. Overton is expected to face Senate confirmation, with some senators expressing concerns about her qualifications and policies.

Overton has been involved in recent executive actions, including the signing of an order to reduce the number of childhood vaccines recommended for children and to split the MMR vaccine into separate shots. She has also been vocal about her opposition to abortion, describing it as "corrosive" to women and society. Her nomination has drawn criticism from Democrats and some Republicans, who argue that her policies could undermine public health and scientific integrity.

Where the accounts differ

Axios reports that Overton may not offer the reassurance the pharmaceutical industry was looking for and that industry analysts have criticized her nomination. The Guardian and FOX News attribute similar concerns to Overton's stance on abortion and vaccine policies. UPI and Washington Examiner note that Overton's nomination has caused tension within the MAHA movement, with some activists viewing her as too aligned with the traditional public health establishment. The Guardian and FOX News also highlight Overton's role in Trump's executive order on vaccines, which has been criticized by the American Academy of Pediatrics as "dangerous" and "disheartening."

Sources Axios · BBC · UPI · Washington Examiner · FOX News · The Guardian

Five Americans among seven killed in Kenya helicopter crash

A helicopter crash in northern Kenya killed seven people, including five Americans, according to multiple reports. The crash occurred on Wednesday morning while the aircraft was flying from the Loisaba Conservancy to the Ewaso Nyiro area in Samburu County. The Kenya Civil Aviation Authority confirmed the crash and stated an investigation was underway. The helicopter, owned by Lady Lori Helicopters, was operating a charter flight for the travel company &Beyond. The aircraft was a Eurocopter EC130 B4. Rescue and recovery efforts faced challenges due to difficult terrain and an active fire at the crash site.

The U.S. State Department confirmed that five of the deceased were American citizens, including a Florida-based Telemundo TV station manager and a Miami restaurateur. The State Department said it was in contact with local authorities and providing consular assistance. The identities of the victims were not immediately released, though some outlets reported that José Alberto Suárez, a Telemundo executive, and Ecuador's intelligence chief Michele Sensi-Contugi, along with his wife, were among those killed.

Where the accounts differ

CBS News and The Guardian both reported that five Americans were killed, including José Suárez and Roger Duarte. The Guardian also named Michele Sensi-Contugi and his wife, Stephany Holliham Yeaza, as victims. UPI and Just The News reported five Americans were killed but did not specify which individuals. FOX News and BBC also mentioned five Americans, but FOX News referred to José Suárez as a Telemundo executive, while CBS News and The Guardian provided more details about his role. The Guardian and BBC noted that Sensi-Contugi was visiting Kenya as a tourist, a detail not included in CBS News or UPI. The Guardian and BBC also mentioned the death of Sensi-Contugi's wife, while CBS News and UPI did not. The Guardian and BBC provided more context about the helicopter's route and the crash location, while UPI and Just The News omitted some details about the victims.

Sources CBS News · The Guardian · UPI · Just The News · BBC · FOX News

Graham says national security ‘not my thing’ but vows to back Trump’s defense agenda

Sen. Darline Graham Nordone (R-SC) admitted during a debate against Rep. Ralph Norman (R-SC) that she is not well-informed on national security, stating, “I’m not that informed on national security.” She defended President Donald Trump’s defense agenda, saying she supports the military and trusts Trump’s handling of the Iran situation. Graham, running to replace her late brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham, also mentioned her brother’s influence on her views, stating she would follow his policies on defense. Norman, her opponent, argued that Trump’s approach to Taiwan and Iran demonstrates “peace through strength,” which deters antagonistic nations. He criticized Trump’s Iran policy, suggesting the president needs to better inform Americans about the situation.

Graham also faced criticism for misstating South Carolina’s population during the debate, claiming there are 50 million residents, while the actual population is approximately 5.5 million. Norman’s campaign pointed out the error on social media. The debate took place ahead of a Republican primary runoff on August 25, where Graham and Norman will face off for the GOP nomination in South Carolina’s special Senate election.

Where the accounts differ

The Washington Examiner and The Daily Wire both report that Graham admitted to not being informed on national security, but The Daily Wire adds that former Gov. Nikki Haley criticized her for the remark. The Daily Caller and Associated Press describe the same admission, with The Daily Caller noting that Graham “faceplants” in the debate and misstates South Carolina’s population. The ABC News account includes audience boos during Graham’s response and mentions Haley’s criticism, while also noting that Graham later claimed South Carolinians care more about domestic issues than foreign policy. The Washington Examiner and The Daily Wire both mention Trump’s endorsement of Graham, while The Daily Caller and ABC News include details about Trump’s comments on other politicians.

Sources Washington Examiner · The Daily Wire · The Daily Caller · Associated Press · ABC News

No source labeled left covered this story.

Disney, ABC file suit against Trump's FCC for retaliation against it

The Walt Disney Company and ABC have filed a lawsuit against the Federal Communications Commission (FCC), alleging the Trump administration is engaging in a retaliatory campaign against the network for its programming. The suit claims the FCC ordered an early license renewal for Disney’s eight owned-and-operated stations, which are not due for renewal until 2028. The lawsuit argues this action is an "existential threat" and part of a broader effort to punish ABC for its content. The suit was filed in a Washington, D.C., federal court, requesting an immediate block on FCC actions related to the early renewal process and a speedy hearing. The complaint also references President Trump’s social media posts criticizing ABC and its late-night programming, including a 2025 post where he suggested revoking broadcast licenses for networks that criticize him.

Where the accounts differ

UPI and The Daily Caller both mention Trump’s 2025 social media post about revoking licenses for networks that criticize him, while Straight Arrow News and Slate refer to a similar post from December 2025. The Daily Caller and The Daily Wire include details about FCC Chairman Brendan Carr’s investigation into Disney’s diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) practices, which UPI and NPR do not mention. The Daily Wire and Slate provide more context about the suspension of Jimmy Kimmel’s show in September 2025, which is omitted by UPI and The Daily Caller. Straight Arrow News and The Daily Wire both note that Carr launched an investigation into ABC’s DEI programs, while UPI and NPR do not specify the nature of the investigation.

Sources UPI · Straight Arrow News · The Daily Wire · Slate · NPR · The Daily Caller

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

Boyfriend of Hayden Panettiere was at apartment when actor died

Hayden Panettiere’s on-and-off boyfriend Brian Hickerson and his brother, Zach Hickerson, were at the South Carolina apartment where the actor died over the weekend, according to a police report. The report states that a Greenville police officer met the brothers upon arrival and observed paramedics performing CPR on an unresponsive woman. The officer noted the patient did not appear to have any obvious physical reasons for being unresponsive. After attempts at lifesaving measures, Panettiere was declared dead at 2:31 p.m. No cause has been determined, and her death remains under investigation. An autopsy found no signs of trauma, and police said they saw no signs of foul play. Panettiere and Hickerson had a tumultuous relationship, with allegations of physical abuse. Hickerson was charged in 2020 with multiple counts of felony abuse and pleaded no contest to two counts of injuring a spouse or partner. He served a short time in jail and was sentenced to four years of probation and anger management. He recently asked a judge to reduce his conviction to misdemeanors, but the request was denied. Panettiere wrote about her decision to forgive Hickerson in her memoir.

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian and CBS News both state that Zach Hickerson identified Panettiere as his brother’s girlfriend, while The Daily Caller and Straight Arrow News do not mention this identification. The Guardian and CBS News note that Brian Hickerson showed the responding officer a bag of medication, while The Daily Wire and The Daily Caller do not mention this detail. The Guardian and CBS News report that the responding officer observed Zach Hickerson being very emotional while EMS worked on Panettiere, while The Daily Wire and The Daily Caller do not specify the emotional reactions of the brothers. The Guardian and CBS News mention that the police report is heavily redacted, while The Daily Wire and The Daily Caller do not mention redactions. The Guardian and CBS News report that the police report was obtained by CBS News, while The Daily Wire and The Daily Caller do not mention how the report was obtained.

Sources The Guardian · CBS News · The Daily Wire · The Daily Caller · Straight Arrow News

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

Russian missile barrage kills at least 13 people in Ukraine’s Kyiv

Russian forces launched ballistic missile attacks on Kyiv, killing at least 13 people and wounding 33, according to Ukrainian officials. Explosions were reported across several districts, including Sviatoshynskyi, Solomianskyi, and Shevchenkivskyi, with a nine-storey residential building collapsing and catching fire in Solomianskyi. A children’s hospital in the district was also damaged. Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko reported that parts of the districts were without electricity and that people were trapped in another residential building. Ukraine’s Emergency Services confirmed at least 33 people were wounded in the attack. In the Brovary district of the Kyiv region, one person was killed and another wounded. Russia’s Ministry of Defence claimed it shot down 726 Ukrainian UAVs between Wednesday evening and Thursday morning.

The attacks prompted security responses in neighboring NATO countries, with Poland mobilizing aircraft and Romania scrambling jets after detecting aerial targets near the Ukrainian border. Ukraine’s new defence minister, Yevhenii Khmara, was confirmed by parliament, with Zelenskyy calling the appointment a sign of increased strength. Zelenskyy also appealed for more anti-ballistic missile support, citing a shortage of Patriot interceptors and the need for Ukraine’s FREYJA program to be operational by 2027.

Where the accounts differ

Al Jazeera and The Guardian both report that at least 13 people were killed, while ABC News and BBC report at least 12 and 13 respectively. Al Jazeera and The Guardian mention the collapse of a nine-storey residential building and damage to a children’s hospital in Solomianskyi, while ABC News and BBC do not specify which buildings were hit. ABC News and BBC report that Zelenskyy called the attack “massive” and described it as one of the most brutal, while Al Jazeera and The Guardian do not include this characterization. The Guardian and BBC mention the use of hypersonic missiles and specific types of Russian weaponry, which are not detailed in Al Jazeera or ABC News. ABC News and BBC report that Ukraine’s air force did not specify how many ballistic missiles were intercepted, while Al Jazeera and The Guardian do not mention this detail.

Sources Al Jazeera · ABC News · The Guardian · BBC
