Trump signs executive order to cut childhood vaccines recommendations, drawing medical concern

President Donald Trump signed an executive order Monday to reduce the number of vaccines recommended for children, sparking widespread concern among the medical community. The order, which calls for limiting vaccines for other diseases to high-risk populations, still recommends childhood vaccines for 11 diseases, including measles and polio. Trump claimed without evidence that childhood vaccines are linked to an increase in autism diagnoses. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who was present for the signing, has maintained this stance as well. The order also advises breaking up the MMR vaccine for measles, mumps and rubella into three separate vaccines. Vaccine advocates and researchers have warned that reducing childhood vaccine recommendations will make children more vulnerable to disease.

Major U.S. medical associations and American doctors were quick to rebuke the executive order as a rejection of science at a time when the United States is experiencing its largest measles resurgence in more than three decades. The National Foundation for Infectious Diseases said in a statement that the nation should be strengthening its ability to protect children, not putting that progress at risk. The American Medical Association criticized the executive order, stating that decisions about how and when vaccines are used should be driven by rigorous scientific evidence, patient safety and independent medical and public health expertise.

Where the accounts differ

UPI reports that the executive order still recommends vaccines for 11 diseases, including measles and polio, while FOX News states that the order recommends vaccines for 11 diseases, fewer than the 18 current CDC guidelines. The Daily Wire and The Guardian both mention that the order reduces the number of diseases from 18 to 11, but The Guardian specifies that only six of the 17 vaccines currently recommended for all children would continue to have full recommendations. CBS News and Axios do not specify the exact number of diseases but both mention the MMR vaccine being split into three separate shots. UPI and The Guardian note that the MMR vaccine is not deadly, while Trump claimed it could be "quite lethal." FOX News and The Daily Wire attribute the claim about the MMR vaccine being "quite lethal" to Trump, while UPI and The Guardian attribute it to Trump as well.

Sources UPI · FOX News · The Daily Wire · The Guardian · CBS News · Axios

Progressive insurgents Francesca Hong and Abdul El-Sayed test Bernie Sanders-style populism in 2026 midterms

Progressive Democrats Francesca Hong and Abdul El-Sayed are running for statewide office in 2026, testing the viability of a leftward shift in the party’s platform. Hong, a state representative in Wisconsin, is leading in the Democratic primary for governor, while El-Sayed, a former public health official, is the Democratic nominee for Senate in Michigan. Both candidates are seen as potential 2028 presidential hopefuls, with their campaigns viewed as experiments in embracing a more radical form of populism. Hong has emphasized affordability and opposed data center construction, while El-Sayed has pushed for Medicare for All and other progressive policies. Their campaigns are closely watched by party leaders who are divided on whether such a leftward turn can succeed in a general election.

Hong’s campaign has faced scrutiny over past social media posts, including calls to “cancel Thanksgiving” and “defund then abolish” the police. She has since walked back these statements, claiming she has “evolved.” El-Sayed, meanwhile, has distanced himself from the “democratic socialist” label, though he has supported policies like abolishing ICE and expanding Medicare. Both candidates are navigating the challenge of balancing progressive ideals with the need to appeal to a broader electorate, particularly as Republicans are actively promoting their campaigns in the general election.

Where the accounts differ

Axios reports that Hong told Politico that a win in November could signal to candidates that working-class issues are a priority. Washington Examiner states that Hong has walked back her 2020 call to “cancel Thanksgiving” and her 2019 and 2021 calls to “defund then abolish” the police. New York Post notes that Hong disavowed her anti-law enforcement positions when confronted with her past statements. The Daily Wire and The Free Press both highlight Hong’s past calls to “defund then abolish” the police and her 2020 tweet about canceling Thanksgiving. Straight Arrow News mentions that Axelrod called Hong “a font of zany liberal, faculty lounge exotica,” while Axios describes her as a “self-described democratic socialist.”

Sources Axios · Washington Examiner · New York Post · The Daily Wire · The Free Press · Straight Arrow News

No source labeled left covered this story.

Iran threat prompted secret Trump flight from Turkiye: Reports

President Donald Trump secretly switched planes during his departure from Turkey last month, using a catering truck to transfer to a smaller military aircraft, according to multiple U.S. media reports. The maneuver was reportedly triggered by a credible Iranian assassination threat. Trump initially stated he would depart on the older Air Force One, but he was instead moved to a C-32A military jet. The Washington Post and The New York Times reported that the older Air Force One served as a decoy, with journalists and some White House staff unaware of the switch. Trump later appeared on the older aircraft in the UK, though the exact method of his transfer from the C-32A to the Air Force One remains unclear. White House Communications Director Steve Cheung defended the new Air Force One, calling it a state-of-the-art aircraft with high-level security protocols.

Where the accounts differ

Al Jazeera and Newsweek both report that Trump was moved via a catering truck to a C-32A aircraft, with the older Air Force One serving as a decoy. However, Newsweek adds that Trump initially stated there was no security concern and that the Qatari-gifted jet had been sent ahead for American service members to tour. CBS News and BBC both mention that the Secret Service advised Trump to take the older plane for security reasons, a detail not included in Al Jazeera or Newsweek. FOX News and BBC note that Trump was seen boarding the older Air Force One in Ankara, but FOX News adds that the legacy jet initially appeared on radar without a call sign before taking the "AF1" call sign midflight, a detail not mentioned in other accounts. The Washington Examiner and CBS News both cite the Washington Post as the source of the report, while BBC and FOX News also reference the Post but add specific details about the operation, such as the involvement of War Secretary Pete Hegseth boarding the C-32A separately.

Sources Al Jazeera · Newsweek · Washington Examiner · FOX News · BBC · CBS News

Timeline: Issues abound after Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool renovations

The Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool faced multiple issues following a multi-million dollar renovation. The project, initially promoted by President Donald Trump, led to disputes over the cause of damage to the pool’s surface. Federal prosecutors, led by U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro, moved to dismiss a felony charge against former Olympian David Hearn, who was accused of vandalizing the pool. The motion cited evidence that the damage was the result of flawed installation by the contractor. Trump, however, continued to claim that the damage was caused by vandals, despite acknowledging there was "no video or proof" of such acts. The pool also experienced algae blooms and peeling of the new protective coating, prompting National Park Service crews to clean the area and apply hydrogen peroxide to the water.

The renovation, which included repainting the pool’s basin in "American flag blue," was initially estimated to cost $1.5 million to $2 million and take a week. However, the final cost reached $16 million, and the project took months to complete. A lawsuit was filed by the Cultural Landscape Foundation, arguing that the blue paint violated federal law by altering the design intent of the National Mall. The pool was eventually reopened after a series of repairs and adjustments, though issues persisted, including peeling and a tear in the sealant.

Where the accounts differ

Straight Arrow News and The Guardian both mention that the Cultural Landscape Foundation filed a lawsuit against the Interior Department, citing the blue paint as a violation of federal law. The Guardian adds that the pool was drained and repainted as part of a beautification push tied to America’s 250th anniversary celebrations. ABC News and The Guardian note that the Justice Department moved to dismiss the case against Hearn, acknowledging the damage was due to a botched installation. FOX News and The Guardian both cite a National Park Service employee as a "highly credible witness" who allegedly saw Hearn "violently" rip and tug at the pool’s coating, though FOX News provides more specific details about the employee’s account and the court documents. Straight Arrow News and ABC News both mention that Hearn denied damaging the pool and claimed he was only checking the liner, but ABC News adds that Hearn’s lawyers described the case as "continued harassment."

Sources Straight Arrow News · Washington Examiner · FOX News · ABC News · The Guardian · NPR

Wildfires Spread Rapidly in Pacific Northwest and Western Canada

Wildfires are spreading rapidly in the Pacific Northwest and western Canada, with extreme fire behavior reported in several regions. The National Interagency Fire Center (NIFC) reported 101 new fires on August 9, including nine large fires, with nearly 30,000 firefighters battling 98 uncontained large fires. The Northwest remains the most active fire region in the U.S., with 46 uncontained large fires burning in Washington and Oregon. In British Columbia, a state of emergency was declared as more than 100 wildfires burned, with the Bald Range fire being labeled "out of control." The fire forced thousands to evacuate, including 12,000 in Summerland and 8,000 in Peachland. A woman died while attempting to flee the fire, according to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.

In Oregon, the Wrights Spring Fire has burned 46,769 acres and remains 0% contained, with 555 firefighters assigned to the incident. The fire prompted evacuations and road closures, and a contract dozer operator, Jason Ensign, died while supporting suppression efforts. In Washington, the Little Giant Fire has burned 116,956 acres and destroyed 26 structures, with 1,813 personnel assigned to the incident. The fire is one of several major incidents in the region, with extreme fire behavior reported.

Where the accounts differ

Newsweek reports that the Wrights Spring Fire burned 46,769 acres and that Jason Ensign died while operating a bulldozer. NPR states that the Wrights Spring Fire burned 33,000 acres and that Jason Ensign died battling the fire. The Guardian and UPI mention the death of an 80-year-old woman during the Bald Range fire evacuation, while BBC and Straight Arrow News also report the woman's death. The Guardian and BBC note that the Bald Range fire burned 53 sq miles, while UPI states it was 13,618 hectares (approximately 53 sq miles). NPR and UPI both mention the Widemouth 2 fire in Utah, with NPR stating it burned 118,000 acres and UPI confirming the same figure. The Guardian and BBC report that the Bald Range fire was 0% contained, while UPI states it was labeled "out of control."

Sources Newsweek · NPR · The Guardian · UPI · BBC · Straight Arrow News

No source labeled lean-right or right covered this story.

Max Miller locked in for reelection bid after Ohio ballot deadline passes

Rep. Max Miller (R-OH) will continue to run for reelection after the 4 p.m. Monday certification deadline passed, despite allegations of domestic violence made against him by his ex-wife, Emily Moreno. Miller is now locked in as the Republican nominee, as Ohio law required county party chairs to notice a nominating meeting at least two days in advance. He has denied the allegations, which include claims of scalding Moreno with hot water, holding a gun to her head, and fracturing their daughter’s collarbone. Democrats view the race as increasingly competitive, with Brian Poindexter, a union ironworker, as the likely Democratic candidate. Recent polls show Poindexter leading Miller by 8 points, though Trump won the district by 11 points in 2024. Miller has called for a House Ethics Committee investigation into himself.

Where the accounts differ

The Washington Examiner and ABC News both state that Miller was never criminally charged in connection with the dispute, while The Daily Caller and FOX News mention that Miller accused his ex-wife of fabricating the allegations due to her mental illness. The Washington Examiner and ABC News report that the Department of Children and Family Services did not find evidence to substantiate child abuse allegations, while The Daily Caller and FOX News include specific details about the alleged incidents, such as scalding Moreno with hot water from a skillet and breaking their daughter’s collarbone. The Daily Caller and ABC News note that Miller’s ex-wife, Emily Moreno, told police that her daughter received physical injuries while in Miller’s care, which is not mentioned in the Washington Examiner or FOX News accounts.

Sources Washington Examiner · NPR · FOX News · ABC News · The Daily Caller

No source labeled left covered this story.

Scores dead in Colombia after powerful earthquake strikes west of country

A powerful 7.4-magnitude earthquake struck western Colombia on Monday, causing widespread damage and resulting in at least 111 deaths. The quake, which occurred at 7:34 a.m. local time, had its epicenter in the western department of Chocó. The US and Colombian geological surveys confirmed the magnitude and location. The president of Colombia, Abelardo de la Espriella, declared a national state of emergency, stating that 111 people had been killed and 87 injured, with 61 buildings collapsed. The hardest-hit cities included Cali, Pereira, and Manizales, where significant damage was reported. Authorities in Cali reported at least 20 buildings collapsed, while Pereira's mayor said 65 buildings had collapsed, with victims trapped in at least 15 of them. The earthquake was felt in neighboring countries including Venezuela, Ecuador, and Panama.

The earthquake caused extensive damage to infrastructure, with reports of collapsed buildings, damaged hospitals, and disrupted transportation systems. Search-and-rescue operations were underway, with residents and emergency crews working to locate survivors. In Manizales, the mayor warned against returning to damaged buildings and urged people to stay outside due to the risk of aftershocks. Social media videos showed the aftermath, including collapsed buildings and people searching for victims in the rubble.

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian and BBC report different death tolls, with The Guardian stating 111 deaths and BBC reporting at least 132. The UPI and BBC also differ on the number of collapsed buildings, with UPI citing 86 buildings collapsed and BBC reporting 65 in Pereira. The Guardian and NPR both mention 111 deaths, while UPI and BBC report higher numbers. The Guardian and BBC attribute the death toll to different sources, with The Guardian citing the president's statement and BBC reporting from local authorities. The UPI mentions 132 deaths according to the Colombian Association of Capital Cities, which is not mentioned in other accounts. The Straight Arrow News reports 70 deaths, which is lower than the other outlets. The Associated Press reports 111 deaths, aligning with The Guardian and NPR, but also mentions over 2,700 people missing, which is not included in other accounts.

Sources The Guardian · NPR · UPI · Straight Arrow News · Associated Press · BBC

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

Below the fold — the model's one nomination, reason printed: Hotel staff's failure to secure room keys led to a woman's assault, exposing systemic vulnerabilities in hospitality safety protocols.

Woman assaulted after Travelodge staff gave room key to her abuser

A woman was assaulted by her domestic abuser after Travelodge staff gave him a key to her room. The woman, who remains anonymous, told the BBC she was staying at a London branch of the hotel in October 2025 to escape her abuser. She said the man, who she described as her abuser, entered the hotel and told reception staff he was the boyfriend of a woman staying there, asking for her room number and floor. He was given a key and directed to her room, where he kicked in the door, assaulted her, and tried to grab her phone. The woman ran downstairs, shaking and crying, and was offered another room in the hotel. Travelodge has acknowledged the incident, stating that their room access security policies were not correctly followed and that they have since made changes to strengthen these policies.

Another woman, Jo from Leeds, told BBC News she was attacked in her Travelodge room in July. She said an unknown man entered her room, and her friend heard him say, “I'm sorry, they gave me this key.” Jo criticized Travelodge’s assurances about safety, saying they were not accurate. Travelodge responded by stating that an investigation found their updated security policies were not followed and that they had retrained staff on current procedures.

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian reports that the woman was staying at the hotel in London in October 2025 and that the abuser told reception staff his girlfriend was having a seizure. The Guardian also mentions a previous case in Maidenhead in 2022 where a man was sentenced to more than seven years in jail after being given a key to a woman’s room and sexually assaulting her. The BBC does not mention this specific case but includes quotes from Jo, a woman from Leeds, and Andy Smith, a frequent Travelodge guest who claims he was given keys to other people’s rooms. The Guardian attributes the statement about the Maidenhead case to the Travelodge spokesperson, while the BBC attributes it to a BBC News report.

Sources The Guardian · BBC · Travelodge

No source labeled lean-left or lean-right or right covered this story.

The brief ends here.

Trump’s Iran War Is Going Backward

On Saturday, a senior Iranian national security official issued a set of demands that the US must meet before a key waterway for oil shipping can be reopened. Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr, the secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, called for the US to lift its sanctions and naval blockade on Iran, “completely compensate” Iran for war damages, “unconditionally” release frozen Iranian assets, and end all attacks on Iran’s allies in the region. According to multiple media outlets, the US government did not deliver an immediate response to the demands. Many of them resemble those in the interim ceasefire deal signed by the US and Iran in June. Back then, the Trump administration said that it would only lift sanctions completely if the two countries came to an agreement on Iran’s nuclear development. While there was an initial ceasefire, it did not last. A couple of days later, Iran’s military closed the Strait of Hormuz, a critical oil transit point, stating the US violated their agreement by allowing Israel to continue bombing Lebanon. Combat resumed and even expanded to Saudi Arabia and the Houthis in Yemen.

Where the accounts differ

Mother Jones and Straight Arrow News both report that Zolghadr listed the same conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz, including lifting sanctions, ending the naval blockade, and compensating Iran for war damages. However, Straight Arrow News adds that Zolghadr also demanded the US end aggression against Iran, Lebanon, Palestine, Yemen, and Iraq, and withdraw its naval and air forces from Iran. The Washington Examiner and New York Post also mention these additional demands, while The Hill and UPI do not. The Hill reports that Vice President Vance said the US is “in the middle of the game” with Iran, while the New York Post and Straight Arrow News attribute this statement to Vance as well. The Washington Examiner and New York Post also note that Trump claimed the negotiations were going “very well” and a deal could be “soon,” a claim not mentioned in Mother Jones or Straight Arrow News.

Sources Mother Jones · The Hill · Straight Arrow News · Washington Examiner · New York Post · UPI

Netanyahu Rejects Trump’s Gaza Plan: No Withdrawal Until Hamas Gives Up ‘All Weaponry’

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu rejected President Donald Trump’s 15-point plan for Gaza, stating that Israel will not withdraw from the territory until Hamas is fully disarmed. Netanyahu emphasized that the Israeli military will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas surrenders all its weapons, including heavy and light arms. He said the two sides are still discussing the matter, with some ideas acceptable and others unacceptable to Israel. Trump had promoted the plan as a historic agreement for the complete disarmament of Hamas and other armed groups in Gaza, with a phased process involving Israeli withdrawal and the establishment of a new Palestinian administration under U.S. supervision.

The plan, negotiated with Arab mediators in Cairo and overseen by Trump’s Board of Peace, outlined a phased process for Hamas to surrender weapons, disclose tunnel locations, and allow a new Palestinian administration to take control. Israeli forces would leave only after areas were verified as demilitarized. Netanyahu, however, insisted that full disarmament must come first, and Israeli troops would not withdraw beyond current lines until Hamas’s weapons are fully decommissioned. The Israeli military has scaled back attacks since a meeting with the Board of Peace’s representative, Nikolay Mladenov, on Monday.

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian reports that Netanyahu’s comments were directed at the U.S. and that Israel has continued attacks on Gaza despite the October 2025 ceasefire. The Daily Wire and UPI mention that Israel has scaled back attacks since meeting with Mladenov, while The Daily Caller and Straight Arrow News include statistics on Palestinian casualties and the International Criminal Court’s arrest warrants for Netanyahu and Yoav Gallant. The Guardian and The Daily Wire note that Netanyahu is facing elections in October, while The Daily Caller and Straight Arrow News include quotes from Hamas officials about expecting the U.S. to pressure Netanyahu. The Daily Wire and The Guardian attribute the characterization of the plan as “genuine disarmament” to Netanyahu, while The Daily Caller and Straight Arrow News attribute it to Netanyahu as well.

Sources The Daily Wire · The Guardian · NPR · Straight Arrow News · UPI · The Daily Caller

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

Woman, baby die after vessel overturns in New York Harbor

A vessel carrying 14 people overturned in New York Harbor near Liberty Island, resulting in the deaths of a woman and her 5-month-old baby. Authorities confirmed the boat's captain, Manuel Hernandez, was arrested for reckless endangerment. The New York Police Department responded to the incident around 10:25 p.m. to 10:55 p.m. on Saturday. Twelve people were rescued from the water before police arrived, with the woman and baby later found and taken to NYU Langone Hospital, where they were pronounced dead. Survivors were reported to have minor injuries and were taken to hospitals in stable condition. The Coast Guard is investigating whether the vessel operated illegally as a charter.

Where the accounts differ

CBS News and UPI both identified the woman as Sara Sanchez and the baby as Antonella Garcia, while FOX News and The Daily Wire did not release their identities. UPI and the New York Post mentioned that the baby's father, who was Sanchez's boyfriend, was also on the boat, a detail not included in CBS News or FOX News. The New York Post and Straight Arrow News reported the boat was 21 feet or 22 feet long, while CBS News and UPI described it as a 2019 21-foot white Yamaha AR210 runabout. The New York Post and Straight Arrow News noted the boat was dangerously overloaded, a claim not made by CBS News or UPI. FOX News and The Daily Wire reported the boat was a 22-foot bowrider, while CBS News and UPI described it as a 21-foot runabout. The New York Post and Straight Arrow News stated the boat overturned around 10:30 p.m., while CBS News and UPI reported the time as 10:55 p.m. and 10:25 p.m., respectively.

Sources CBS News · FOX News · UPI · Straight Arrow News · New York Post · The Daily Wire

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

Trump says Will Scharf will replace David Warrington as White House counsel in September

President Donald Trump announced that White House Staff Secretary Will Scharf will replace David Warrington as Assistant to the President and White House Counsel starting September 1. Trump praised Scharf for his legal background, including his work as a federal prosecutor and his representation of Trump in multiple cases, including at the Supreme Court. Scharf, who previously served as chair of the National Capital Planning Commission, oversaw the approval of Trump’s $400 million White House ballroom project. The White House counsel’s role includes advising on legal and policy matters, coordinating with the Justice Department, and managing congressional investigations.

The White House counsel’s office is central to the administration’s legal strategy, handling presidential pardons, judicial appointments, and reviewing legislation. Scharf, who joined Trump’s legal team in October 2023, was involved in the presidential immunity case that led to the Supreme Court’s ruling in favor of Trump. The appointment comes amid preparations for the midterm elections, with Democrats vowing to pursue investigations into Trump and his administration if they gain control of Congress.

Where the accounts differ

The Washington Examiner and The Guardian both mention that Scharf will replace Warrington effective September 1, while The Daily Wire and UPI state the effective date as September 1 as well. The Washington Examiner and ABC News note that Warrington is leaving for the private sector, though the Washington Examiner does not specify his new role, while ABC News and The Guardian describe him as returning to private practice. The Daily Wire and UPI mention that Scharf was part of the legal team that argued for Trump’s immunity in the Supreme Court case, while The Guardian and ABC News attribute this to Scharf’s involvement in the case. The Washington Examiner and The Guardian both mention Scharf’s role in the National Capital Planning Commission, but The Washington Examiner adds that he led the commission, while The Guardian states he chaired it. The Daily Wire and UPI note that Scharf warned against suspending habeas corpus protections for illegal immigrants, a claim not made by The Guardian or ABC News.

Sources Washington Examiner · The Daily Wire · ABC News · UPI · The Guardian · Al Jazeera

Crews battle wildfires in western U.S. and Canada

Wildfires are spreading rapidly across the western U.S. and Canada, with evacuation orders in place for multiple regions. The National Interagency Fire Center reported 183 new fires, including eight large ones, across the U.S. since Saturday, with over 30,000 personnel and 640 crews assigned to the fires. In Utah, the Rocky Canyon Fire has grown to over 2,800 acres and is 0% contained, leading to evacuations in Morgan County. Two pilots died in a helicopter crash while battling the Widemouth 2 Fire in Fishlake National Forest, and the fire has scorched over 118,000 acres, becoming the largest in Utah this year. In Oregon, a bulldozer operator died while fighting the Wrights Spring Fire, which has spread over 33,000 acres. In Canada, British Columbia has seen over 100 wildfires, with the Bald Range wildfire prompting more than 20,000 people to evacuate. A state of emergency was declared in the province, and officials warned of "explosive" fire conditions due to prolonged drought and high temperatures.

Where the accounts differ

NPR and CBS News both report that the Widemouth 2 Fire has scorched over 118,000 acres and is the largest fire in Utah this year, surpassing the Babylon Fire. However, CBS News also mentions that the Bald Range wildfire has scorched more than 53 square miles, while BBC and UPI report it as 13,618 hectares (33,650 acres). The Guardian and CBS News state that an 80-year-old woman died while trying to escape the wildfire, while UPI and Washington Examiner confirm this death and attribute it to the Bald Range wildfire. The Guardian and CBS News also mention that the Bald Range fire was first detected late on Friday evening and grew to more than 40 sq miles within hours, while NPR and Washington Examiner report it as first reported Friday evening and growing to about 50 square kilometers within hours.

Sources NPR · The Guardian · CBS News · BBC · UPI · Washington Examiner

No source labeled right covered this story.

Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez announces decision to freeze her eggs

Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, a 36-year-old New York congresswoman, announced she is freezing her eggs and will share the process online. She described the decision as a way to feel more in control of her life. Ocasio-Cortez shared the process through Instagram stories, showing the medication and tools used, including syringes and alcohol wipes. She injected herself in the dressing room before an ABC interview, stating that women can do anything and that it is “badass” to take such shots. She also mentioned the importance of normalizing conversations about women’s health, especially in a political environment where reproductive care is under threat.

Ocasio-Cortez emphasized the lack of information available to women about their bodies and reproductive health. She highlighted the challenges of balancing personal and political life, noting that being in the public eye at a young age means navigating major life decisions in the spotlight. She also mentioned the financial and technological advancements that have made egg freezing more accessible. Ocasio-Cortez hinted at the possibility of running for president in 2028, though she said the focus should remain on the midterm elections.

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian and The Daily Wire both mention Ocasio-Cortez’s comments about the political “risk” of sharing her decision, while FOX News and The New York Post attribute similar statements to her. The Washington Examiner notes that Ocasio-Cortez has not ruled out a 2028 presidential run, a detail not included in The Guardian or BBC accounts. The Daily Wire and The New York Post describe Ocasio-Cortez as having been engaged to Riley Roberts since 2022, a detail absent from other accounts. The Guardian and The Daily Wire include quotes from Amanda Litman and Xochitl Hinojosa, which are not present in the Washington Examiner, BBC, or FOX News reports.

Sources The Guardian · Washington Examiner · The Daily Wire · BBC · FOX News · New York Post

No source labeled lean-left covered this story.

Shanghai cancels 1,300 flights as China prepares for Typhoon Dolphin

Typhoon Dolphin, which brought heavy rains to northern Taiwan, prompted authorities in China to cancel over 1,300 flights in Shanghai and relocate more than 300,000 people in surrounding regions. The storm’s outer bands hit northern Taiwan, including Taipei, on Saturday. Shanghai’s Hongqiao and Pudong airports canceled about 60% of Sunday’s expected flights. Authorities in Zhejiang province evacuated 390,000 people in Taizhou by Saturday evening and 900,000 in Wenzhou. In Fujian, 98,900 people were evacuated from high-risk areas. Forecasters warned of severe flooding and landslide risks, with some areas expected to receive 200-400 mm of rainfall over the next few days.

Authorities in Shanghai evacuated 30,000 people from riskier areas and suspended all water-based activities, including ferries and cruises. The storm’s maximum sustained winds were estimated at about 162 km/h (101 mph) as of Sunday morning. The National Meteorological Centre warned that the storm could slow over central and southwestern China, prolonging heavy rainfall and increasing flood and landslide risks.

Where the accounts differ

Al Jazeera reports that Typhoon Dolphin made landfall near Yuhuan in Zhejiang province at 5:30pm on Sunday, with maximum sustained winds of 151 km/h (93 mph), equivalent to a Category 1 hurricane. This differs from the Associated Press, which states the storm’s maximum sustained winds were estimated at about 162 km/h (101 mph) as of Sunday morning. The Guardian also reports landfall at 5:30pm with 151 km/h winds, while UPI mentions landfall at Force 13 speeds of 85 mph. The Guardian also notes that Shanghai evacuated 215,600 people, substantially higher than the 30,300 figure cited by Al Jazeera and the BBC. The BBC mentions that Shanghai canceled nearly 1,000 flights, while the Associated Press and the Guardian report 1,300 and 1,500 flights canceled respectively.

Sources Associated Press · Al Jazeera · BBC · The Guardian · UPI · The Guardian

No source labeled lean-right or right covered this story.

Below the fold — the model's one nomination, reason printed: Salmonella outbreak linked to jalapeños could hospitalize thousands, prompting recalls and economic losses for farmers.

Some meat products with jalapeños may be linked to salmonella outbreak, USDA says

Federal officials issued a public health alert for meat and poultry products containing jalapeños that may be contaminated with salmonella, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture. The alert applies to products regulated by the Food Safety and Inspection Service (FSIS) that may have been affected by a recalled ingredient. The USDA said it learned of the issue when it discovered that multiple FSIS-regulated establishments had received a recalled ingredient. The agency released a list of 18 recalled products, including brands like Taylor Farms, Ready Meals, Meal Simple, Higher Harvest, and Deli Kitchen. The USDA noted that additional downstream products may be identified as the ingredient recall progresses.

The salmonella outbreak was first reported in mid-June and is linked to jalapeño peppers grown in Sinaloa, Mexico, and distributed by Coast Citrus Distributors. As of Aug. 5, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reported that at least 345 people in 27 states had been sickened, with 36 hospitalized. Minnesota was particularly hard hit, with at least 110 cases confirmed. Of 191 patients interviewed, 93% reported eating at a Mexican-style restaurant before falling ill, including Chipotle and Qdoba. Both chains removed jalapeños from their menus. Albertsons voluntarily recalled four items containing jalapeños supplied by Taylor Farms.

Where the accounts differ

CBS News states that the USDA said there have been "no confirmed reports of illness" from FSIS-regulated products containing jalapeños sourced from Sinaloa. Straight Arrow News reports that FSIS said there have been "no confirmed illnesses tied specifically to the FSIS-regulated meat and poultry products containing the recalled jalapeños." CBS News also notes that the first illnesses were reported in mid-June and links them to jalapeños from Sinaloa, while Straight Arrow News attributes the outbreak to "fresh jalapeño peppers grown in Sinaloa, Mexico." CBS News mentions that Albertsons recalled four items, while Straight Arrow News states that the public health alert includes products sold under several brands and distributed through major retailers and convenience stores.

Sources CBS News · Straight Arrow News

No source labeled lean-right or left or right covered this story.

The brief ends here.
